title: Searching a Concatenated Value Blocks the Seek
description: Concatenating columns to compare (first + ' ' + last) can't seek; compare the underlying indexed columns instead.
narrative:
## Scenario
A "search by full name" feature runs `WHERE FirstName + ' ' + LastName = 'John Smith'` against a 200,000-row `Customers` table that already has a composite index on `(LastName, FirstName)`. The index is never used.

## Why it's slow
`FirstName + ' ' + LastName` is an **expression computed from the columns** — the engine can't know which index entry equals `'John Smith'` without first building the concatenation for **every** row. That makes the predicate **non-sargable**, so SQL Server falls back to a full **Index Scan** and evaluates the concatenation as a residual filter.

## What to look for
- An **Index Scan** (not a Seek) on `Customers`, reading all 200k rows.
- The concatenation appearing as a Compute Scalar / residual predicate rather than a seek predicate.

## The concept
Anything that wraps the indexed columns — a function, arithmetic, or a **concatenation** — hides the raw values the index is sorted on. Compare the columns **individually** (`FirstName = 'John' AND LastName = 'Smith'`) and the composite index seeks straight to the rows. Same result, a scan of 200k rows becomes a handful of reads.
hints: The predicate compares a concatenation, not the columns themselves — the index can't seek on a value it must compute per row.
Split the search into the underlying columns so each can be matched against the index key.
Use WHERE FirstName = 'John' AND LastName = 'Smith'; — the (LastName, FirstName) index now seeks.
